Unsupervised Learning: Trade & Ahead¶

Problem Statement¶

Context¶

The stock market has consistently proven to be a good place to invest in and save for the future. There are a lot of compelling reasons to invest in stocks. It can help in fighting inflation, create wealth, and also provides some tax benefits. Good steady returns on investments over a long period of time can also grow a lot more than seems possible. Also, thanks to the power of compound interest, the earlier one starts investing, the larger the corpus one can have for retirement. Overall, investing in stocks can help meet life's financial aspirations.

It is important to maintain a diversified portfolio when investing in stocks in order to maximise earnings under any market condition. Having a diversified portfolio tends to yield higher returns and face lower risk by tempering potential losses when the market is down. It is often easy to get lost in a sea of financial metrics to analyze while determining the worth of a stock, and doing the same for a multitude of stocks to identify the right picks for an individual can be a tedious task. By doing a cluster analysis, one can identify stocks that exhibit similar characteristics and ones which exhibit minimum correlation. This will help investors better analyze stocks across different market segments and help protect against risks that could make the portfolio vulnerable to losses.

Objective¶

Trade&Ahead is a financial consultancy firm who provide their customers with personalized investment strategies. They have hired you as a Data Scientist and provided you with data comprising stock price and some financial indicators for a few companies listed under the New York Stock Exchange. They have assigned you the tasks of analyzing the data, grouping the stocks based on the attributes provided, and sharing insights about the characteristics of each group.

Data Dictionary¶

  • Ticker Symbol: An abbreviation used to uniquely identify publicly traded shares of a particular stock on a particular stock market
  • Company: Name of the company
  • GICS Sector: The specific economic sector assigned to a company by the Global Industry Classification Standard (GICS) that best defines its business operations
  • GICS Sub Industry: The specific sub-industry group assigned to a company by the Global Industry Classification Standard (GICS) that best defines its business operations
  • Current Price: Current stock price in dollars
  • Price Change: Percentage change in the stock price in 13 weeks
  • Volatility: Standard deviation of the stock price over the past 13 weeks
  • ROE: A measure of financial performance calculated by dividing net income by shareholders' equity (shareholders' equity is equal to a company's assets minus its debt)
  • Cash Ratio: The ratio of a company's total reserves of cash and cash equivalents to its total current liabilities
  • Net Cash Flow: The difference between a company's cash inflows and outflows (in dollars)
  • Net Income: Revenues minus expenses, interest, and taxes (in dollars)
  • Earnings Per Share: Company's net profit divided by the number of common shares it has outstanding (in dollars)
  • Estimated Shares Outstanding: Company's stock currently held by all its shareholders
  • P/E Ratio: Ratio of the company's current stock price to the earnings per share
  • P/B Ratio: Ratio of the company's stock price per share by its book value per share (book value of a company is the net difference between that company's total assets and total liabilities)

Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)¶

  • EDA is an important part of any project involving data.
  • It is important to investigate and understand the data better before building a model with it.
  • A few questions have been mentioned below which will help you approach the analysis in the right manner and generate insights from the data.
  • A thorough analysis of the data, in addition to the questions mentioned below, should be done.

Questions:

  1. What does the distribution of stock prices look like?
  2. The stocks of which economic sector have seen the maximum price increase on average?
  3. How are the different variables correlated with each other?
  4. Cash ratio provides a measure of a company's ability to cover its short-term obligations using only cash and cash equivalents. How does the average cash ratio vary across economic sectors?
  5. P/E ratios can help determine the relative value of a company's shares as they signify the amount of money an investor is willing to invest in a single share of a company per dollar of its earnings. How does the P/E ratio vary, on average, across economic sectors?

# function to plot a boxplot and a histogram along the same scale.


def histogram_boxplot(df, feature, figsize=(12, 7), kde=False, bins=None):
    """
    Boxplot and histogram combined

    data: dataframe
    feature: dataframe column
    figsize: size of figure (default (12,7))
    kde: whether to the show density curve (default False)
    bins: number of bins for histogram (default None)
    """
    f2, (ax_box2, ax_hist2) = plt.subplots(
        nrows=2,  # Number of rows of the subplot grid= 2
        sharex=True,  # x-axis will be shared among all subplots
        gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": (0.25, 0.75)},
        figsize=figsize,
    )  # creating the 2 subplots
    sns.boxplot(
        data=df, x=feature, ax=ax_box2, showmeans=True, color="violet"
    )  # boxplot will be created and a star will indicate the mean value of the column
    sns.histplot(
        data=df, x=feature, kde=kde, ax=ax_hist2, bins=bins, palette="winter"
    ) if bins else sns.histplot(
        data=df, x=feature, kde=kde, ax=ax_hist2
    )  # For histogram
    ax_hist2.axvline(
        df[feature].mean(), color="green", linestyle="--"
    )  # Add mean to the histogram
    ax_hist2.axvline(
        df[feature].median(), color="black", linestyle="-"
    )  # Add median to the histogram
# function to create labeled barplots


def labeled_barplot(data, feature, perc=False, n=None):
    """
    Barplot with percentage at the top

    data: dataframe
    feature: dataframe column
    perc: whether to display percentages instead of count (default is False)
    n: displays the top n category levels (default is None, i.e., display all levels)
    """

    total = len(data[feature])  # length of the column
    count = data[feature].nunique()
    if n is None:
        plt.figure(figsize=(count + 1, 5))
    else:
        plt.figure(figsize=(n + 1, 5))

    plt.xticks(rotation=90, fontsize=15)
    ax = sns.countplot(
        data=data,
        x=feature,
        order=data[feature].value_counts().index[:n].sort_values(),
    )

    for p in ax.patches:
        if perc == True:
            label = "{:.1f}%".format(
                100 * p.get_height() / total
            )  # percentage of each class of the category
        else:
            label = p.get_height()  # count of each level of the category

        x = p.get_x() + p.get_width() / 2  # width of the plot
        y = p.get_height()  # height of the plot

        ax.annotate(
            label,
            (x, y),
            ha="center",
            va="center",
            size=12,
            xytext=(0, 5),
            textcoords="offset points",
        )  # annotate the percentage

    plt.show()  # show the plot

Sectors with Positive Price Change

  • Information Technology: High Likely driven by tech demand, AI, or digital transformation.

  • Consumer Staples: High Typically resilient during economic uncertainty.

  • Utilities: Moderate Stable returns, often seen as safe investments.

  • Financials: Moderate May reflect interest rate dynamics or banking sector strength.

  • Real Estate: Slight Possibly recovering from prior downturns.

  • Materials: Slight Could be linked to industrial demand.

Sectors with Negative Price Change

  • Energy: Significantly Negative Sharp decline, possibly due to falling oil prices or regulatory pressure.

  • Telecommunications Negative with High Variability Wide error bars suggest uncertainty or mixed performance.

  • Consumer Discretionary: Slightly Negative May reflect cautious consumer spending.

  • Industrials: Near Zero Flat performance, possibly due to global supply chain issues.

numerical_cols = df.select_dtypes(include=np.number).columns
plt.figure(figsize=(15, 8))
sns.boxplot(data=df[numerical_cols])
plt.xticks(rotation=90)
plt.show()

  • Current Price: Few Some stocks have unusually high or low prices.

  • Price Change: Few A few stocks show abnormal daily changes.

  • Volatility: Few Some assets are significantly more volatile.

  • ROE : Few A few companies have exceptionally high or low ROE.

  • Cash Ratio Few Some firms hold unusually high or low cash reserves.

  • Net Cash Flow Many: High variability in operational or investment cash flow.

  • Net Income Many Wide spread in profitability across companies.

  • Earnings Per Share Few Some firms have unusually high or low EPS.

  • Estimated Shares Outstanding: Many Large differences in company size or share structure.

  • P/E Ratio Few Some stocks are priced disproportionately to earnings.

  • P/B Ratio Few A few firms have book values far from market values.

  1. Feature engineering
  • Let`s Create a new DataFrame df_num by selecting only the numerical columns from the original DataFrame df that are suitable for clustering. Exclude identifier columns such as 'Ticker Symbol' and 'Security'.
In [34]:
numerical_cols = df.select_dtypes(include=np.number).columns
excluded_cols = ['Ticker Symbol', 'Security', 'GICS Sector', 'GICS Sub Industry']

# Filter out any excluded columns that might have been picked up as numerical (e.g., if they were encoded numerically)
clustering_numerical_cols = [col for col in numerical_cols if col not in excluded_cols]

df_num = df[clustering_numerical_cols].copy()
print("DataFrame with only numerical columns for clustering (df_num) created.")
df_num.head()

  • Let`s visualizing the distribution of 'P/E Ratio' in the scaled data.
In [40]:
histogram_boxplot(df_scaled, 'ROE')

The data suggests that while a few companies achieve high ROE, the majority operate with modest returns. The presence of many outliers and skewness implies that using the median might be more representative than the mean for central tendency.

  • Let`s visualizing the distribution of P/E Ratio
In [41]:
histogram_boxplot(df_scaled, 'P/E Ratio')

The dataset is heavily concentrated around low P/E values, with a few extreme outliers. The mean is higher than the median, confirming asymmetry in valuation. This pattern is common in markets where a few growth stocks inflate the average, while most stocks remain modestly valued.

K-means Clustering¶

  1. Checking Elbow Plot
In [42]:
k_means = df_scaled.copy()
In [43]:
clusters = range(1, 15)
meanDistortions = []

for k in clusters:
    model = KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=1, n_init=10)
    model.fit(df_scaled)
    prediction = model.predict(df_scaled)
    distortion = (
        sum(np.min(cdist(df_scaled, model.cluster_centers_, "euclidean"), axis=1))
        / df_scaled.shape[0]
    )

    meanDistortions.append(distortion)

    print("Number of Clusters:", k, "\tAverage Distortion:", distortion)

plt.plot(clusters, meanDistortions, "bx-")
plt.xlabel("k")
plt.ylabel("Average Distortion")
plt.title("Selecting k with the Elbow Method", fontsize=20)
plt.show()

model = KMeans(random_state=1, n_init=10)
visualizer = KElbowVisualizer(model, k=(1, 15), timings=True)

visualizer.show()  # finalize and render figure
Out[44]:
<Axes: title={'center': 'Distortion Score Elbow for KMeans Clustering'}, xlabel='k', ylabel='distortion score'>
  • The optimal number of clusters for this dataset is 𝑘=8, as identified by the elbow method.
  • Choosing 𝑘=8 offers a good trade-off: significant reduction in distortion without excessive increase in fit time
  • Beyond 𝑘=8, additional clusters yield minimal improvement in clustering quality while increasing computational cost.
  1. Let's check the silhouette scores
In [45]:
sil_score = []
cluster_list = range(2, 15)
for n_clusters in cluster_list:
    clusterer = KMeans(n_clusters=n_clusters, random_state=1, n_init=10)
    preds = clusterer.fit_predict(df_scaled)
    score = silhouette_score(df_scaled, preds)
    sil_score.append(score)
    print("For n_clusters = {}, the silhouette score is {})".format(n_clusters, score))

plt.plot(cluster_list, sil_score)
plt.show()

<Axes: title={'center': 'Silhouette Plot of KMeans Clustering for 340 Samples in 2 Centers'}, xlabel='silhouette coefficient values', ylabel='cluster label'>
  • The clustering with 2 centers yields a strong overall structure, as indicated by the high average silhouette score.
  • Most samples are well-matched to their clusters, with minimal overlap or ambiguity.
  • The presence of a few negative scores is normal and does not significantly detract from the clustering quality.
  • This supports the earlier conclusion that 𝑘=2 is a valid and effective choice for this dataset, offering clear separation and compactness.

Hierarchical Clustering¶

  1. Computing Cophenetic Correlation
In [56]:
hc_df = df_scaled.copy()
In [57]:
# list of distance metrics
distance_metrics = ["euclidean", "chebyshev", "mahalanobis", "cityblock"]

# list of linkage methods
linkage_methods = ["single", "complete", "average", "weighted"]

high_cophenet_corr = 0
high_dm_lm = [0, 0]

for dm in distance_metrics:
    for lm in linkage_methods:
        Z = linkage(hc_df, metric=dm, method=lm)
        c, coph_dists = cophenet(Z, pdist(hc_df))
        print(
            "Cophenetic correlation for {} distance and {} linkage is {}.".format(
                dm.capitalize(), lm, c
            )
        )
        if high_cophenet_corr < c:
            high_cophenet_corr = c
            high_dm_lm[0] = dm
            high_dm_lm[1] = lm

# printing the combination of distance metric and linkage method with the highest cophenetic correlation
print('*'*100)
print(
    "Highest cophenetic correlation is {}, which is obtained with {} distance and {} linkage.".format(
        high_cophenet_corr, high_dm_lm[0].capitalize(), high_dm_lm[1]
    )
)

  1. Checking Dendrograms
In [59]:
# list of linkage methods
linkage_methods = ['single', 'complete', 'average', 'weighted']

# lists to save results of cophenetic correlation calculation
compare_cols = ["Linkage", "Cophenetic Coefficient"]
compare = []

# to create a subplot image
fig, axs = plt.subplots(len(linkage_methods), 1, figsize=(15, 30))

# We will enumerate through the list of linkage methods above
# For each linkage method, we will plot the dendrogram and calculate the cophenetic correlation
for i, method in enumerate(linkage_methods):
    Z = linkage(hc_df, metric="euclidean", method=method)

    dendrogram(Z, ax=axs[i])
    axs[i].set_title(f"Dendrogram ({method.capitalize()} Linkage)")

    coph_corr, coph_dist = cophenet(Z, pdist(hc_df))
    axs[i].annotate(
        f"Cophenetic\nCorrelation\n{coph_corr:0.2f}",
        (0.80, 0.80),
        xycoords="axes fraction",
    )

    compare.append([method, coph_corr])
  • Average linkage yielded the highest cophenetic correlation of 0.9423.
  • Single linkage followed with 0.9232. Weighted linkage was 0.8694.
  • Complete linkage had the lowest correlation at 0.7873.
  • We will move ahead with Average linkage
  • 3 appears to be the appropriate number of clusters from the dendrogram for average linkage

K-means vs Hierarchical Clustering¶

You compare several things, like:

  • Which clustering technique took less time for execution?
  • Which clustering technique gave you more distinct clusters, or are they the same?
  • How many observations are there in the similar clusters of both algorithms?
  • How many clusters are obtained as the appropriate number of clusters from both algorithms?

You can also mention any differences or similarities you obtained in the cluster profiles from both the clustering techniques.

  1. Let`s see clustering technique that took less time for execution
In [89]:
import time
from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans, AgglomerativeClustering

# Generate sample data
X, _ = make_blobs(n_samples=1000, centers=5, n_features=10, random_state=42)

# Timing K-means
start = time.time()
kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=5, random_state=42)
kmeans.fit(X)
kmeans_time = time.time() - start

# Timing Hierarchical Clustering (Agglomerative)
start = time.time()
hierarchical = AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=5)
hierarchical.fit(X)
hierarchical_time = time.time() - start

print(f"K-means execution time: {kmeans_time:.4f} seconds")
print(f"Hierarchical execution time: {hierarchical_time:.4f} seconds")

K-means execution time: 0.0075 seconds
Hierarchical execution time: 0.0626 seconds

Based on calculation time between K‑means and hierarchical clustering:

  • K‑means took less time for execution. This is because K‑means iteratively updates cluster centroids.
  • Hierarchical clustering requires computing and storing all pairwise distances, which grows quadratically with dataset size.
  1. The clustering technique that gave me more distinct clusters, or are they the same?

Based on the analysis of cluster distinctness:

  • Hierarchical Clustering (with Euclidean distance and average linkage) appears to offer a more faithful representation of the data's inherent structure and potentially more distinct clusters, as indicated by its very high cophenetic correlation of 0.9423. This suggests that the distances between data points are well-preserved in the hierarchical structure.

  • K-means Clustering (with 3 clusters) provides reasonably distinct clusters, as shown by its silhouette score of 0.4644. While acceptable, this score suggests that there might be some data points that are not as clearly assigned to their clusters or that the clusters might be somewhat less separated compared to what the hierarchical method suggests.

  1. Let`s see the number of observations there are in the similar clusters of both algorithms

Comparison of Cluster Sizes and Company Distribution:¶

K-means Clustering (3 Clusters):

  • Cluster 0: Contains 262 companies.
  • Cluster 1: Contains 16 companies.
  • Cluster 2: Contains 62 companies.

K-means produced one very large cluster (Cluster 0) and two smaller clusters (Cluster 1 and 2), indicating a highly imbalanced distribution. Most companies fall into one broad category, with a few outliers forming distinct, smaller groups.

Hierarchical Clustering (3 Clusters):

  • Cluster 0: Contains 337 companies.
  • Cluster 1: Contains 1 company.
  • Cluster 2: Contains 2 companies.

Hierarchical clustering, with 3 clusters, resulted in an even more imbalanced distribution. One cluster (Cluster 0) is exceptionally large, encompassing almost all companies, while Cluster 1 and Cluster 2 are tiny, representing only 1 and 2 companies, respectively. This suggests that the hierarchical algorithm, when forced into 3 clusters, identifies a few extreme outliers as separate clusters.

  1. Based on the analysis, here's how the appropriate number of clusters was determined for each algorithm:

For K-means Clustering:

  • Elbow Method (Distortion Score): The elbow method, while somewhat ambiguous, suggested an optimal number around 8 clusters.

Silhouette Score:

  • The silhouette score analysis indicated that 3 clusters yielded the highest average silhouette score of 0.4644, suggesting better-defined clusters. However, the final K-means model was built and profiled with 2 clusters, which also showed a reasonably good silhouette score and was chosen for a more general comparison.

For Hierarchical Clustering:

  • Cophenetic Correlation: The highest cophenetic correlation (0.9423) was obtained using 'Euclidean' distance and 'average' linkage, indicating a faithful representation of the data's structure.

Dendrogram: Visual inspection of the dendrogram suggested that 3 main clusters would be appropriate.

Actionable Insights and Recommendations¶

K-Means Clustering Insights (2 Clusters):¶

Cluster 0 (Larger Cluster - 337 Companies):

  • These companies generally exhibit average price changes, lower volatility, and moderate financial metrics (ROE, Cash Ratio, Net Income, EPS, P/E, P/B). They seem to represent a stable, broad market segment with balanced performance.
    • Insight: This cluster likely contains a mix of established companies with consistent performance, potentially offering steady growth and moderate risk. They might be suitable for investors seeking balanced portfolios.

Cluster 1 (Smaller Cluster - 3 Companies):

  • This cluster stands out with significantly negative price changes, high volatility, and extremely high ROE. While the average cash ratio is moderate, they show very low Estimated Shares Outstanding, and P/E and P/B ratios.
    • Insight: This cluster points to a group of highly volatile, potentially distressed or highly speculative stocks. The high ROE might indicate specific accounting events or a turnaround situation, but the negative price change and high volatility suggest high risk. These could be high-risk, high-reward opportunities or value traps.

Hierarchical Clustering Insights (3 Clusters):¶

Cluster 0 (Largest Cluster - 337 Companies):

  • Similar to K-means Cluster 0, these companies show moderate financial performance across the board, with average price changes and volatility. They form the bulk of the market.
  • Insight: This cluster represents the general market trend with diverse companies. Strategies here would need further sub-segmentation or fundamental analysis.

Cluster 1 (Smallest Cluster - 1 Company - 'Priceline.com Inc'):

This cluster contains a single company with a very high current price, but otherwise average metrics. The P/E and P/B ratios are very low in comparison to its current price, implying that the valuation might be underpriced. * Insight: This represents a unique outlier, possibly a high-growth stock that is currently undervalued or has a high absolute price due to historical factors.

Cluster 2 (Small Cluster - 2 Companies - 'Apache Corporation', 'Chesapeake Energy'):

  • These companies are characterized by very low current prices, significant negative price changes, extremely high volatility, and exceptionally high ROE. They also have relatively low Cash Ratio, Net Cash Flow and Net Income.
  • **Insight:** This cluster represents highly distressed or speculative energy-related companies.
